categorical

/kat-uh-GOR-ih-kuhl/ - the stress falls on GOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Categorical means absolute and without exceptions — said of statements, denials, and rules.

The chef's ban on shortcuts is categorical: no bottled dressing, no frozen dough, and no exceptions on busy nights.

Example

The allergy clinic's rule is categorical: no peanut products cross the threshold — not in lunches, not in sealed wrappers, not for the staff party — and in nine years the director has granted zero exemptions.

Categorical means absolute — admitting no exceptions, no conditions, no 'unless.' A categorical refusal doesn't say 'probably not' or 'not this time'; it closes every door at once, which is why the word attaches so naturally to denials, bans, and guarantees.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unconditional: Unconditional means offered with no conditions attached — nothing the receiver must first do or keep doing — and it is said of support, surrender, and love. Categorical belongs instead to statements: a categorical denial or ban admits no exceptions. Gifts and backing are unconditional; denials and rules are categorical.

outright: Outright means complete and total — an outright lie, an outright ban, an outright victory — stressing that the thing is fully itself, nothing partial about it. Categorical adds the idea of no exceptions even in principle: a categorical denial closes every door at once, future cases included.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hedged: wrapped in qualifications and escape clauses

noncommittal: deliberately refusing to take a clear position

Where it sits · how completely exceptions are ruled out — firm → unwavering → categorical

firm vs. categorical: Firm is milder than categorical — a firm no can still soften under enough pressure, the way a categorical one never does.

unwavering vs. categorical: Unwavering comes close but stops short of categorical — an unwavering stance holds steady over time, while a categorical refusal also rules out every exception in advance.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — categor-

Root — categor-: to assert publicly, to accuse (Greek kategorein)

Suffix — -ical

Suffix — -ical: relating to

Put it together

Put it together: Categor- (Greek kategorein, 'to assert or accuse before the assembly') + -ical = of outright assertion. From the same verb, Greek philosophers coined kategoria — a 'category,' the class you assign a thing to by stating plainly what it is. Something categorical is declared the way a category is: flatly, completely, nothing left conditional.

Use the root in a new word: category

Use the root in a new word: category: The librarian shelves each donation by category — fiction, history, or science — before it ever reaches the cart.

Word Choice

formal

Categorical is the formal word for absolute statements: a categorical denial, ban, or guarantee. In speech, plain 'flat' or 'absolute' often serves — but when you want to stress that no exception exists even in principle, categorical says exactly that, which is why lawyers and press offices love it.
